content.thinking:
I'm planning out a whimsical low-poly gnome figure around 1.1m tall, sketching the body structure with hips, spine, chest, neck, head, and limbs as a connected chain.

I'm deciding to use explicit world-space coordinates for each bone rather than local offsets to keep things simpler and less error-prone, and starting to sketch helper functions for building rounded body parts like a ball geometry for joints.

For the character design, I'm planning the head with a large nose, goggle-style eyewear, and a layered white beard built from stacked cone shapes mirrored left-to-right for a stylized tinkerer look, keeping the total part count well under the limit.

Still designing geometry...

Setting up leg chains with hip, knee, ankle, and toe joints mirrored for each side.

Adding boot cuff and sole details...

Now I'm placing shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand joints for the arm chain, positioning them further out and down the body for a relaxed resting pose.

Setting up hands with mitt-shaped spheres plus thumb and finger capsules rigidly attached to the wrist bone, skipping separate digit joints since they aren't essential. I'm also designing a backpack frame mounted on the spine behind the figure—a boxy leather body with patches, positioned low on the back.

Now I'm working out the shoulder strap sweeps: since the torso is roughly radius 0.15 wide and 0.12 deep, I'm orienting the sweep radius so width maps to the binormal and depth to the normal, then plotting catmull-rom points running from the pack top over the shoulder down to a front belly strap, keeping the path clear of the torso surface.

Checking strap positioning against torso cap curvature, computing where it crosses the shoulder ellipse surface and continuing down to the front point near the chest.

Now mapping the belt as a closed catmull ring at the waist, using an elliptical ring of points to form a smooth loop around the torso.

For the character's colors, I'm settling on a whimsical palette: tomato red hat, teal tunic, mustard trousers, brown boots, leather backpack, and brass accents for buckles and hardware.

For the backpack, I'm designing it as the real centerpiece—a pack frame with flap and side pockets, a bedroll cylinder on top, a telescoping brass telescope sticking out diagonally, and a copper gear cluster on the back built from an extruded gear outline that needs careful point generation to avoid self-intersection.

I'm also layering on an antenna with a spring-wrapped ball tip, hanging tools like a wrench and hammer, a screwdriver poking out, a glowing lantern on the side, coiled brass pipes with a dial-faced pressure gauge, and a small hinge-jointed propeller mounted on a mast with spinning extruded blades.

Now adding more dangling charm details: a key ring, tin cup, forehead goggles on the hat band, a tool belt with screwdrivers and a pliers pouch, and spiral-swept spring coils for extra texture.

I'll pass bone consistently throughout. For the texture dial, I'm thinking of an SVG gauge with ticks and a needle on a plane facing backward since the pack sits on the back. For the chest emblem, I'm considering using a decal function targeting the torso sweep directly, positioned at the front of the chest facing outward, which could also work for the eyes.

Simpler spheres with pupils will work better for the eyes than decals. For the hat, I'm building it as a catmull-rom sweep curve bending back and sideways toward a tip, with a tapering radius function and a small bobble sphere at the top, anchored to the head bone starting where the head sphere's top surface sits.

I'm checking that the hat's radius clears the head geometry at the base, then adding a lathed brim just below the hat's base using a profile outline that curves outward and back in for a natural brim shape.

With the hat sitting flat above the face, I'm checking that brims and eyebrows don't collide with the eyes, then sketching the head shape itself—a faceted low-poly sphere with pointed cone ears and a round nose sphere positioned on the face.

Still placing facial features...

Working out the hat band and goggle strap placement, I'm placing a dark leather band ring around the hat at roughly y 1.015 with radius .167, then positioning the goggle strap so lenses rest just above it at y 1.03.

Now I'm sketching a reusable ring helper for closed catmull curves, then moving to the beard: a thick white sweep curving down from the chin area with a tapering radius profile to form the gnome's facial hair, with a mustache layer over the mouth.

Adding spike strands fanning from the beard tip, then painting the beard with a cream grain texture. I'm also sweeping a mustache shape near the nose, checking it sits just below the nose geometry without overlapping.

I'll skip the mouth and lips since the beard covers that area, and focus on fluffy white eyebrow sweeps instead. I'm adjusting the hat brim and base height so it clears the eyebrows and sits properly on the head without colliding with the hat radius.

I'm checking that the hat cone encloses the head top at various heights and placing the goggles just above that, with the ears peeking out below the brim. Now I'm working on the tunic coloring, planning a teal base with mottled countershading and hem trim stripes.

For the apron I'm shaping a leather front piece as a tapered box draped from chest to knees, sizing its width and depth sections, and adding pocket patches, brass rivets, and a printed detail.

I'm reconsidering whether to skip the skirt and let the apron cover the hips instead, adjusting the torso's radius profile at each height to form a believable pelvis bulge and belly curve.

Still working out the arm and shoulder widths, and planning sleeve coloring in bands -- teal for the rolled-up upper sleeve transitioning to cream near the forearm.

Working out the leg bands so pants transition into boots at the shin, with chunky boot radii widening near the ankle for a sturdier look.

For the feet, I'm positioning the toe tip and ankle tube so the foot stays grounded within tolerance, and adding a flat darker sole box underneath for a more defined base.

Now I'm working out the skeleton joint coordinates — placing the hips, spine path, chest cap, neck, and chin positions so the torso curves naturally upward from hips to head.

Checking the belt and arm clearance from torso, then sizing gloves with cuff details. Legs look fine, so I move to the backpack and gadget placement, positioning the pack behind the shoulders and head with enough depth clearance, and extending taller gadgets like telescopes above and beside the head without clipping.

Now I'm constructing the backpack itself: a boxy leather body with mottled texture, a tilted top flap with brass buckle straps, a darker base, small side pockets with flaps, and a horizontal bedroll cylinder attached.

Still writing geometry setup...

Defining gear tooth geometry...

Rerouting the pipe path along the right edge to avoid the gear, with flanged brass joints, then sketching a telescope accessory as three tapering nested cylinders angled diagonally off the left side of the pack.

Now I'm adding sphere joints at the pipe's bends, a glowing cyan eyepiece lens cap, and a right-top antenna rod with a red glowing tip bobble, plus working out a lathe profile for a small satellite dish to mount near the antenna base.

I'm also positioning a hinged propeller mast above the backpack, checking its blade radius against nearby antenna and telescope parts to avoid collisions.

Positioning the propeller at the back-bottom of the pack as a pinwheel rotating around the Z axis, checking clearance against the gears, then defining the hub and blade geometry in the plane perpendicular to that axis.

Now adding more accessories hanging off the pack: an antenna up top, a lantern on the left, a tin cup, and small tools like a hammer and wrench clipped to the sides, with the wrench outline built from a handle rectangle plus a notched jaw shape.

Still mapping wrench geometry...

Still placing the gear, gauge, and propeller positions, then trying to fit the wrench somewhere it won't collide with the pipes or pack pocket—considering hanging it along the pack's side surface instead of the bottom.

Working out the wrench's orientation hanging from the belt, checking it fits between the thigh and arm without collision, then setting up the hammer shape on the opposite hip with its handle and head outline.

Now I'm placing the hammer on the left side (s=-1) opposite the wrench, and adding small leather pouches at the front of the belt with flaps and rivets.

I'm figuring out the front belt layout: two pouches near the center, a buckle with a gear badge, and an apron that sits below the beard so it stays visible beneath the beard's tip while leaving room for the straps at the sides.

To avoid z-fighting with the straps, I'll drop the apron bib and keep only a lower apron skirt hanging from the belt, between waist and hip height, sized to flare slightly outward like a work apron -- floating just in front of the thighs but visually anchored by the belt. I'll add pocket patches and rivets for detail.

Since the beard hides a chest badge, I'll place a decal instead on the hat's front-left, using a projected ray onto the hat surface for a small gear-patch icon (rendered as an SVG with a circle and teeth shapes). I'm also considering a paper tag decal on the pack for extra detail.

Thinking about additional pack decorations, I'll add a rolled blueprint scroll as a small tan-and-blue cylinder tied to the pack's side, and maybe a couple of round sewn-patch planes stuck onto the pack front, each using a small square plane with a patch-style decal texture.

I'm also planning a hanging lantern off the left side of the pack, suspended from a short hook arm with a chain, featuring a brass base, glowing amber glass cylinder body, and a conical cap.

Now I'm resolving collisions: moving telescope and lantern apart so the left side holds the telescope and its pocket, while the right side gets the antenna, blueprint tube, and lantern hook, adjusting their x-positions so nothing overlaps.

I'm reconsidering where to strap the blueprint tube -- trying it horizontally under the pack near the hip region at a slightly recessed z-depth so it clears the bedroll and buttocks geometry without intersecting the pack's lower edge.

Now I'm adding a hanging tin cup tool beneath the pack, plus a brass wrist gauge/compass gadget on the left wrist built from a flattened cylinder disc, and considering giving the right hand a small wrench or spanner extruded along the hand's grip direction, pointing forward-up.

Working out the orientation vectors...

I'll give the right hand a glowing screwdriver instead - orange handle, steel shaft, with a tiny spark glowing at the tip. For the left hand, I'll have it hold a small glass bulb glowing yellow on a brass base, sitting right in the palm.

Now let me set up the builder helpers - a sphere geometry function and a `put` helper for placing parts with flat shading, typed against the PartOptions interface. Then I'll start defining the joints, beginning with the hips.

Working through the skeleton structure, I'm defining the spine as a chain following a polyline path from hips through to chest, then adding the neck and head joints with appropriate positions and orientations. For the face, I need a separate upper and lower jaw since the beard will hide the mouth, so I'm placing a jaw joint beneath the head.

Figuring out mouth placement...

Actually the mouth would get overlapped by the beard and mustache geometry no matter where I place it, so I'll skip adding a mouth and just rely on the mustache for facial detail.

I'll split the jaw into its own rig piece: a flattened chin sphere on the jaw joint, with the beard attached there, while the mustache stays fixed to the head joint. The head sphere sits a bit higher, and the jaw sphere sits below it to give the chin some separation.

Now I'm placing the face features: nose protruding slightly in front of the head, eyes offset to each side with their position computed so the sphere surface lines up correctly against the head's curvature, and pupils nested just in front of the eye whites so they peek out slightly without floating free.

I'm also working out the nose's larger rounded shape, cheek blush ellipsoids positioned symmetrically, and the ear spikes attached to the head — thinking through how to avoid z-fighting between the inner pink ear and the outer skin-colored ear by offsetting their geometry.

Now I'm sketching the eyebrows, hat band, and white sideburn tufts, then moving into defining the beard as a swept catmull-rom curve along the jawline with tapering width.

Writing interpolation helper...

I'm checking that the beard's depth and position stay clear of the torso and apron geometry, making sure the tip doesn't overlap the belt area.

Setting beard grain noise size to .02 to avoid streaking, then working out the mustache curve placement against the face surface geometry, checking that the radius at each point clears the beard bar so it protrudes correctly.

Now I'm sizing the hat to sit on the head joint pointing upward, then shifting to the torso sweep profile — defining chest and belly width/depth with a sine taper so the belly bulges wider than the chest, fitting a gnome-like silhouette.

I'm positioning a cream collar ring around the neck at the right height to match the torso's rounded taper, then working out a hem trim band near the bottom where the torso curves back inward.

Now I'm shaping the tunic skirt as a lathed flare that widens enough to cover the legs' top extent, with a brass-colored trim ring circling the hem.

I realize the apron panel sticking out front will collide with the skirt surface since both occupy similar front-z space, so I'm nudging the apron's z-offset and path points outward so it sits flush in front without clipping into the skirt geometry.

Next, I'm placing the belt ring at the torso's mid-height, sizing it to match the torso's cross-section at that y-value, and sitting it just above the skirt's waistline so it doesn't intersect. Then I'm adding a belt buckle as a small brass box with a darker inset slot and a gear-shaped detail, followed by side pouches positioned symmetrically along the belt.

Since the pouches would overlap the apron if placed too centrally, I'm pushing them further out to the hips, planning a pouch box on one side and a hanging tool on the other, each with a flap and a small brass button detail.

For the left hip I'm adding a wrench shape plus a coiled rope rendered as a thin torus near the front. Then I'm moving to the hands, building each as a sphere stretched slightly for shape, with a thumb capsule, a wrist cuff cylinder, and small knuckle spheres positioned along the front to suggest fingers.

I'm sorting out the arm bone chain naming and hierarchy — shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand joints under the chest parent — and resolving how to reference the terminal hand joint for attaching the glove geometry.

Now I'm placing a small compass piece on the left wrist with a glowing lens disc, then moving on to the goggles and hat band positioning, figuring out the surface point and direction vectors along the hat's curved profile.

Positioning the goggles on the hat with lenses centered around y 1.05, sized so the rims and cyan glowing lenses protrude slightly from the brass mounts, connected by a bridge piece and strap rod between them, plus a small brass buckle detail on the hat band.

Now I'm thinking through the hat's coloring using a countershaded mottled red pattern with a darker gradient toward the back, and adding a yellow bobble sphere at the drooping tip of the hat's curved path, positioning the tip point along a catmull curve extending outward and down.

Working out the curve points so the hat droops back and down without colliding with the antenna, then tapering the hat's radius from wide at the base to a thin point at the tip.

Now I'm sketching the pack's body as a box positioned on the back, with vertical rod frames alongside it, building out the backpack geometry piece by piece.

Adjusting the flap placement to sit at the top back with a smaller drop, adding vertical leather straps with brass buckles, and now positioning side pockets while checking for clearance against the telescope attachment.

I keep running into collisions between the telescope, the gauge, and the pocket geometry on the pack's left side, so I'm shifting the telescope outward and angling it diagonally to clear the pocket space, then reworking the arm position to avoid overlapping the telescope's shaft.

Now I'm building the telescope out of segmented rods with varying radii and materials, plus small joint bands and an eyepiece cup, positioning the lens-facing end upward toward the viewer.

I'm adding a glowing lens cap at the top end and two torus-shaped leather mounting straps wrapped around the telescope barrel, then starting a rod for an antenna piece in the upper right.

Now I'm working on a bowl-shaped lathe profile for a small dish at the antenna's tip, defining the outline points so the bowl is concave and opens outward along its axis.

Next I'll add a feed rod extending forward from the dish with a glowing red ball at its tip, plus a coiled spring shape at the antenna's base using a spiral path with specified turns, radius, and pitch.

Then I'm working out the right-side pocket symmetry with a lantern hook: positioning a rod from the pocket to a hanging point, and adding a chain connecting down to the lantern itself.

The lantern construction follows with a cone cap, a hexagonal glass cylinder glowing amber, a base plate, and thin corner posts topped with a ring handle, plus a glowing lens inside to simulate the bulb light. I'm also checking the arm position to confirm the lantern's z-offset fits, then moving to design a brass gauge cylinder mounted on the chest with its own dimensions and orientation.

Now I'm figuring out the gauge's dial plane placement so it faces outward correctly, matching the texture's orientation to the cylinder's back face, and sketching two meshing gears extruded along the depth axis with slightly offset z-centers so their teeth appear to interlock visually.

I'm considering treating the gears and propeller as actual hinge joints in the rig, defining a joint role attached to the chest bone aimed along the depth axis so they can rotate properly, then starting to write a helper function that generates the gear tooth outline points.

Now I'm working out the gear hub details — a cylinder disc with a bolt and small dark spoke holes — and designing the propeller blades as rotated extrusions at 120-degree intervals with a tapered outline shape.

I'm setting the propeller joint with a hinge role, then planning to merge small sphere geometries for rivets and brass studs using a helper function that packs them onto specific bones like the chest and spine.

For the pack gadgetry, I'm figuring out a hanging tin cup using a lathe profile with a hollow shape, positioned near the bottom of the pack and attached via a hook or carabiner.

Now I'm placing a blueprint tube under the pack along the back of the hips, checking its position clears the torso geometry, and adding small leather torus straps to wrap around the tube at either side.

For the side pockets, I'm sizing boxes with flap covers and buttons, textured with LEATHER2, then dressing them up: the left pocket gets a trio of colored screwdriver handles (red, yellow, blue) poking out the top, while the right pocket could hold a flask instead. I'm also considering adding patch decals to the pocket fronts facing outward.

I'll skip adding a boiler/steam stack to the pack since the back is already crowded, and pass on a dangling bell too -- keeping things simpler there. Now I'm roughly tallying up part counts across the head, hat, beard, and torso to gauge model complexity.

Adding a stitched knee patch now: I'm placing a small decal plane at the front of the knee joint where the leg tube bends, calculating its z-position based on the hip-knee-ankle geometry, and texturing it with a pale square patch bordered by dashed stitch lines.

Now I'm sketching out the SVG textures needed - a gauge dial with cream face, tick marks, red zone and needle, plus a round star-badge patch with contrasting stroke colors, making sure stroke widths stay thick enough to render crisply at the chosen texture resolution.

Now I'm switching to the boot geometry, sizing the sole box and positioning it against the toe and heel regions, and considering painted patches or mottled texture for the boots along with small lace boxes crossing the front of the foot near the ankle.

Figuring out where the boot top sits along the leg by computing path lengths from hip to knee to ankle, interpolating position along the shin segment, and landing on a y-coordinate near .133 for the boot's upper edge.

Defining the radius function...

I should double-check the shoulder sphere covers the torso-arm gap, and then focus on avoiding unused-variable typecheck errors by trimming imports down to just what I actually use: mottle, countershade, grain, patches, plus the path and merge utilities.

Defining color palette...

Adding more colors and defining paint effects like countershading on the tunic and stripes on the pants...

Setting up imports and module structure, then adding gear helper functions outside the build function for generating gear outlines...

Setting up the builder with a centering offset, then defining a helper for placing colored geometry and working through the right type for color/paint parameters.

Defining the torso sweep now, tapering the radius along the spine chain so it narrows toward the top, with the skirt covering where the rounded bottom cap dips slightly.

I'm lathing the skirt profile around the hips bone, checking that its top radius stays wider than the torso so it drapes outside cleanly, then adding a hem trim as a thin closed loop swept around the skirt's bottom edge for detail.

Now I'm placing the belt as a ring around the spine1 bone between its joint range, then setting up pack straps anchored to the chest bone before moving into the legs. For the legs, I'm looping over left and right sides, defining hip-knee-ankle-foot points as a polyline rather than a smoothed curve so the joints stay crisp and low-poly, then chaining them into a leg bone hierarchy parented to the hips.

Still writing leg sweep and sole/knee details...

Switching to arms now, I'm defining shoulder-elbow-wrist-hand points as another polyline and chaining them to the chest, then working out sleeve radius bands and taper values for the arm sweep.

Modeling the hand shape with a scaled sphere for the palm, then adding finger capsules extending forward and down from it.

I'm positioning the bulb just above the hand so it looks gripped despite overlapping geometry, placing the glass sphere with a brass base cylinder and giving it a yellow glow plus filament detail.

For the right hand, I'm building a screwdriver prop with an orange capsule handle, a steel shaft angled forward-up, and a small glowing spark tip, then adding wrist cuff cylinders on both arms.

Now I'm sketching the glove colors and placing a compass accessory on the left wrist, angling it to sit flat on top.

Skipping the neck detail since the beard covers it. For straps, I'm using a sweep with a linear taper from thick to thin rather than an ellipse function, approximating a box cross-section along the chest bone.

Now I'm working out the actual strap path coordinates by computing the torso's dome geometry at different heights to figure out where the strap should sit on the surface, both in front and along the back.

Checking the strap's fit against the torso at other heights confirms it stays close enough to the body without clipping, so the ellipse radius and sweep look good overall. Now I need to figure out where the lower anchor point sits on the pack's side-bottom.

I'll move on to loose details like the bedroll cylinder, positioning it at the top with a rotation that aligns its axis horizontally, plus small end discs for the rolled-up look.

Now I'm placing torus straps around the bedroll perpendicular to its axis, verifying their position sits correctly against the pack frame, then checking the frame bars and cross rods don't clip through the bedroll's top.

That edge check against the arm looks fine, and hips are settled too. Now I'm mentally structuring the final code—keeping TypeScript strict with proper types, using for-of loops, and settling on the rod function signature with a color/bone options object. Writing SVG helper functions...

Placing ears with the spike function using base, tip, and radius bone options, skipping fur tufts and beard cards for a cleaner low-poly look. Now I'm positioning the hat sweep with its tapering radius profile along the head bone, plus a badge decal near the hat's front at a specific height and angle.

Adding dark pupil spheres with a small radius and fanning the beard strand spikes at their tips before finalizing and returning the root part.
